lessons.title: A debate: town life or village life?
lessons.objective: Argue for or against town or village life and defend one’s point of view politely.
lessons.course:
In a debate, two teams give reasons for and against an idea. We start with “I think…”, “In my opinion…”, we give reasons with “because”, and we answer the other team politely: “I agree with you, but…”, “I don’t agree because…”.
We speak in turns, we listen, and the chairperson gives the floor.

support.title: Useful phrases
support.text:
In my opinion, village life is better because the air is clean.
I don’t agree, because in town there are hospitals and good roads.
I agree with you, but…

lessons.model: Two adults debate: one says town life is better (electricity, hospitals, jobs), the other says village life is better (clean air, fresh food, family close by).
lessons.guided: Prepare three reasons for your side. Hold a short debate at home or in class with a chairperson.
lessons.exercise: Give one reason why village life can be good.
lessons.answer: For example: the air is clean and the food is fresh.
lessons.remediation: Give one reason with “because” before debating.
lessons.transfer: Ask two adults which they prefer, town or village, and why.

practice.prompt: Which phrase disagrees politely?
Match each reason with the side it supports.
pairs: The air is fresh and clean.

practice.prompt: Say your opinion with a reason.

lessons.title: Reading silently: market day in Kumba
lessons.objective: Read a text silently and answer questions; find synonyms and opposites.
lessons.course:
When we read silently, we read with our eyes, without moving our lips. We read the questions first, then look for the answers in the text.
Synonyms have almost the same meaning (big – large); opposites have contrary meanings (cheap – expensive).

support.title: Read silently
support.text: Wednesday is market day in Kumba. Very early, traders arrive from the villages with plantains, cocoyams and palm oil. The market becomes noisy and crowded. Mrs Mbah sells fresh fish at a fair price, but the imported shoes in the next stall are expensive. By evening, the market is quiet again and the cleaners sweep the alleys.

lessons.model: The adult reads the questions, then reads silently and points to each answer in the text.
lessons.guided: Read the questions, read the text silently and write the answers. Find one synonym and one opposite pair.
lessons.exercise: Which day is market day in Kumba?
lessons.remediation: Read one sentence at a time and ask: who? what? when?
lessons.transfer: Describe your local market day to your family.

practice.prompt: Match each word with its opposite.
What does Mrs Mbah sell?
practice.explanation: The text says she sells fresh fish.

practice.prompt: Find a synonym of “crowded” in the list: full, empty, small.

lessons.title: A persuasive essay: why our town needs a park
lessons.objective: Write a short persuasive essay giving reasons and examples to convince the reader.
lessons.course:
A persuasive essay tries to convince. Plan it:
• Introduction: give your opinion (“Our town needs a public park.”).
• Body: give two or three reasons with examples (“Children need a safe place to play.”).
• Conclusion: repeat your opinion and ask for action (“Let us ask the mayor to build one.”).
Useful words: firstly, secondly, moreover, finally, therefore.
lessons.model: The adult writes the opinion and two reasons on the board, linking them with “Firstly” and “Secondly”.
lessons.guided: Choose a topic (a park, a library, a clean market). Write the opinion, two reasons and a conclusion.
lessons.exercise: Which word can introduce your second reason?
lessons.remediation: Write one opinion sentence and one reason with “because”.
lessons.transfer: Read your essay to an adult and ask whether it convinced them.

practice.prompt: Put the parts of the persuasive essay in order.
items: Firstly, children need a safe place to play.
Therefore, let us ask the mayor to build one.

practice.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason?
choices: Children need a safe place to play.
practice.answer: Children need a safe place to play.

practice.prompt: Write your persuasive essay (about 60 words).
practice.answer: A persuasive essay with an opinion, reasons and a conclusion.

lessons.title: Adjectives: proper adjectives, comparatives and superlatives
lessons.objective: Identify common and proper adjectives and use comparative and superlative forms.
lessons.course:
Common adjectives describe: tall, busy, beautiful. Proper adjectives come from proper nouns and take a capital letter: Cameroon → Cameroonian, Africa → African, England → English.
Comparatives compare two: tall → taller (than), busy → busier, beautiful → more beautiful. Superlatives compare three or more: the tallest, the busiest, the most beautiful.
Irregular: good – better – the best; bad – worse – the worst.
lessons.model: The adult compares: “Douala is bigger than Buea. Douala is the biggest town in the Littoral region.”
lessons.guided: Compare three towns or three buildings with comparatives and superlatives. Write five proper adjectives.
lessons.remediation: Start with short adjectives (tall, small) before longer ones.
lessons.transfer: Compare three things in your village with “-er” and “the -est”.

practice.prompt: Complete the table.
Which one is a proper adjective?
practice.explanation: It comes from Cameroon and takes a capital letter.

practice.prompt: Match each adjective with its superlative.

lessons.title: Intersection and union of sets in the village
lessons.objective: Find the intersection and the union of two sets and use the symbols ∩, ∪ and ∉.
lessons.course:
A = {children who go to the market} = {Ali, Bih, Che}; B = {children who go to the stream} = {Bih, Che, Dzeke}.
Intersection A ∩ B = elements in both sets = {Bih, Che}. Union A ∪ B = all elements of A and B, written once = {Ali, Bih, Che, Dzeke}.
∉ means “is not an element of”: Dzeke ∉ A.
lessons.model: The adult draws two overlapping circles and places the names: the middle part is the intersection.
lessons.guided: Make two sets about activities in your village. Draw them in a Venn diagram and write A ∩ B and A ∪ B.
lessons.remediation: Colour the elements that are in both lists first.
lessons.transfer: Make a Venn diagram of the foods two family members like.
lessons.materials: Two hoops or circles drawn on paper.

practice.prompt: A = {a, b, c}, B = {c, d}. How many elements are in A ∪ B?
practice.explanation: {a, b, c, d}: c is written once.

practice.prompt: Match each symbol with its meaning.
practice.answer: ∩ intersection; ∪ union; ∉ not an element of.

practice.prompt: Draw a Venn diagram of A = {goat, hen, dog} and B = {dog, cat}.
practice.answer: Two circles with “dog” in the middle.
practice.explanation: The common element goes in the intersection.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting up to 5 000 at the market
lessons.objective: Add and subtract four-digit numbers with carrying and borrowing and solve market problems.
lessons.course:
We write numbers in columns (Th H T U) and start with the units. Carry when a column makes 10 or more; borrow when the top digit is smaller.
2 750 + 1 380 = 4 130. 4 000 − 1 275 = 2 725. Check a subtraction with an addition: 2 725 + 1 275 = 4 000.
lessons.model: The adult solves: “Mama sold plantains for 2 350 frs and oranges for 1 475 frs. Total?” in columns: 3 825 frs.
lessons.guided: Solve six market problems in columns. Check each subtraction with an addition.
lessons.remediation: Use bundles and coins to show carrying and borrowing.
lessons.transfer: Add up the cost of three items your family bought at the market.

practice.explanation: Carry in the units, tens and hundreds.

practice.prompt: A trader had 5 000 frs. He spent 2 780 frs. How much is left?
How do we check 4 000 − 1 300 = 2 700?

lessons.title: Perimeter of a rectangle and a square: fencing a garden
lessons.objective: Calculate the perimeter of rectangles and squares.
lessons.course:
The perimeter is the distance all round a shape. Rectangle: P = (length + width) × 2. Square: P = side × 4.
A garden 12 m long and 8 m wide needs (12 + 8) × 2 = 40 m of fence.
lessons.model: The adult walks round a rectangle drawn on the ground and adds the four sides.
lessons.guided: Measure the perimeter of a book, a table and a room. Use the formulas and check by adding the four sides.
lessons.exercise: A square field has sides of 15 m. What is its perimeter?
lessons.remediation: Add the four sides one by one before using the formula.
lessons.transfer: Calculate how much rope is needed to go round your compound’s garden.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 5 cm wide. Perimeter in cm?
Which formula gives the perimeter of a square?
practice.explanation: A square has four equal sides.

practice.prompt: A fence of 40 m goes round a square pen. How long is one side, in m?

lessons.title: Grid references and coordinates on a village map
lessons.objective: Locate places on a map using a grid and coordinates.
lessons.course:
A grid divides a map into squares. Columns have letters (A, B, C…) and rows have numbers (1, 2, 3…). The school is in square C2: column C, row 2.
On a coordinate grid, we read across first, then up: the point (3, 4) is 3 across and 4 up.
lessons.model: The adult draws a village map on a 5 × 5 grid and finds the church at B4 and the well at (2, 1).
lessons.guided: Draw a grid map of your quarter with five places. Write their grid references.
lessons.exercise: On a coordinate grid, how do we read (5, 2)?
lessons.remediation: Use a grid on the floor and walk across, then up.
lessons.transfer: Make a treasure map with grid references for a friend.

practice.prompt: We read coordinates…
practice.explanation: Along the corridor, then up the stairs.

practice.prompt: The point (4, 3) moves 2 squares up. What is its new second number?
Draw a grid map of your quarter with five places.
practice.answer: A map with grid letters and numbers.
practice.explanation: Write the reference of each place.

lessons.title: Domestic and wild animals around the village
lessons.objective: Differentiate domestic from wild animals, describe their habitats and practise their care and conservation.
lessons.course:
Domestic animals live with people and depend on them: goats, sheep, cattle, pigs, dogs, cats, hens. Wild animals live freely in nature: monkeys, antelopes, elephants, crocodiles, porcupines.
A habitat is the place where an animal lives and finds food, water and shelter: forest, savannah, river, swamp, a farm.
We care for domestic animals (food, water, shelter, vaccination) and protect wild animals (no hunting of protected species, no burning of their forests).
lessons.model: The adult shows two pictures: a goat in a pen and a monkey in the forest, and asks where each finds food.
lessons.guided: Make a table of ten animals: domestic or wild, habitat, food. Name one animal protected in Cameroon’s parks (for example the elephant or the gorilla).
lessons.exercise: Is a porcupine domestic or wild?
lessons.remediation: Ask: Does it live with people? Who gives it food?
lessons.transfer: Observe a domestic animal at home and say how it is cared for.

practice.prompt: Match each animal with its habitat.
practice.answer: crocodile: river; monkey: forest; goat: farm.

practice.prompt: Which one is a domestic animal?
Give one way to protect wild animals.
practice.answer: For example: do not burn the forest.

lessons.title: Décrire une personne : il est grand, elle est gentille
lessons.objective: Décrire une personne : son aspect physique et son caractère.
lessons.course:
Pour l’aspect physique : « Il est grand / petit. Elle est mince. Il a les cheveux courts. Elle a des tresses. »
Pour le caractère (aspect moral) : « Il est gentil / sympa. Elle est joyeuse. Il est timide. Elle est courageuse. »
Attention : un garçon gentil, une fille gentille ; un homme courageux, une femme courageuse.

support.title: Mots utiles
support.text:
grand(e), petit(e), mince, fort(e)
gentil / gentille, sympa, joyeux / joyeuse, timide, courageux / courageuse

lessons.model: L’adulte décrit le chef du quartier : « Il est grand et fort. Il a une barbe blanche. Il est sage et gentil. »
lessons.guided: Décris une personne de ton village en quatre phrases : deux sur le physique, deux sur le caractère. Ton partenaire devine qui c’est.
lessons.remediation: Travaille deux adjectifs au masculin et au féminin.
lessons.transfer: Décris un ami en français à ta famille.

practice.prompt: Relie le masculin et le féminin.
Quelle phrase décrit le caractère ?
Complète avec est ou a.
practice.text: Il [[est]] grand. Il [[a]] les cheveux courts.
practice.explanation: être pour l’adjectif ; avoir pour les cheveux.

lessons.title: Authorities of our region
lessons.objective: Identify state, traditional and religious authorities, explain the administrative structure of a region and respect each authority.
lessons.course:
Cameroon is divided into 10 regions. A region is divided into divisions, and divisions into subdivisions.
State authorities: the Governor (region), the Senior Divisional Officer (division), the Divisional Officer (subdivision), the mayor (council). Traditional authorities: Fons, chiefs, Lamibé, quarter heads. Religious authorities: bishops, pastors, imams, priests.
Each authority has a role: maintain order, settle disputes, organise development, guide believers.
lessons.model: The adult draws a chart: Region → Division → Subdivision, with the authority of each level.
lessons.guided: Find the name of your region, division and subdivision, and of one traditional authority of your area.
lessons.remediation: Learn the three levels first: region, division, subdivision.
lessons.transfer: Ask an adult the name of your mayor and your quarter head.
lessons.materials: A map of the regions of Cameroon.

practice.prompt: Match each unit with its authority.
How many regions does Cameroon have?
Which one is a traditional authority?
practice.explanation: Fons and chiefs are traditional authorities.

lessons.title: Rearing snails and rabbits
lessons.objective: Feed and care for small livestock such as snails and rabbits and keep their cages clean.
lessons.course:
Snails need a shady, humid pen with soft soil, fresh leaves (cassava, pawpaw), fruit peels and a little calcium (crushed eggshells) for their shells. They must not dry out.
Rabbits need a dry, clean hutch raised from the ground, fresh grass and leaves, clean water every day, and a quiet place. We clean cages regularly and wash our hands after.
lessons.model: The adult visits a small snail pen and a rabbit hutch and explains feeding and cleaning.
lessons.guided: Draw a snail pen and a rabbit hutch and label food, water and shelter. Write a weekly care plan.
lessons.exercise: What do snails need for their shells?
lessons.remediation: Compare one need at a time: food, water, shelter.
lessons.transfer: Visit someone who rears small animals and ask two questions.
lessons.materials: Pictures of a snail pen and a hutch.

practice.prompt: Match each animal with its shelter.
practice.answer: snails: pen; rabbits: hutch; poultry: coop.

practice.prompt: What do rabbits need every day?
practice.explanation: Rabbits need water and fresh food.

practice.prompt: Write a weekly care plan for rabbits.
practice.answer: A plan with feeding, water and cleaning.
practice.explanation: Say what to do each day.

lessons.title: Traditional and modern instruments of our village and town
lessons.objective: Distinguish traditional musical instruments from modern ones and play an instrument of one’s choice.
lessons.course:
Traditional instruments are made from local materials: the balafon (wooden keys and gourds), the tom-tom and the slit drum (wood and skin), the mvet (a stringed instrument of the South), rattles and bells.
Modern instruments are made in factories: the guitar, the keyboard, the trumpet, the drum kit. Many bands mix both.
lessons.model: The adult plays a rhythm on a tom-tom, then on a plastic bucket, and compares the sounds.
lessons.guided: Sort pictures of instruments into traditional and modern. Make a rattle or a simple drum and play a rhythm.
lessons.exercise: Is the balafon traditional or modern?
lessons.remediation: Ask: Is it made from local materials?
lessons.transfer: Ask an elder which instruments are played at ceremonies in your village.
lessons.materials: Pictures, tins, seeds, a bucket, sticks.

practice.prompt: Match each instrument with its kind.
What is a balafon made of?
practice.explanation: The balafon is a wooden xylophone.

practice.prompt: Play a rhythm: long, short, short, long.

lessons.title: Sprinting 50 metres and keeping speed
lessons.objective: Run faster over a given distance and maintain speed to the finish.
lessons.course:
For a 40–60 m sprint: a quick start (crouch or standing), drive with the arms, run on the balls of the feet, look straight ahead, keep the speed and run through the finish line.
We time races in seconds. Rest between sprints.
lessons.model: The adult runs 50 m while a partner times with a watch or by counting.
lessons.guided: Mark 50 m. Run three sprints with rest. Note your times and see if you improve.
lessons.exercise: Where must you slow down: before or after the finish line?
lessons.transfer: Time a sprint with friends and encourage each other.
lessons.materials: Stones to mark the track, a watch.

practice.prompt: Bih ran 50 m in 10 s, 9 s and 8 s. What was her best time in seconds?
practice.explanation: The smallest time is the best.

practice.prompt: Which part of the foot do we run on?

lessons.title: A traditional marriage ceremony
lessons.objective: Identify elements of culture related to marriage and traditional dressing and dramatise a traditional marriage.
lessons.course:
In many cultures, a traditional marriage brings two families together: the visit of the groom’s family, the presentation of gifts (often called the bride price or dowry, depending on the culture), speeches by elders, the blessing, songs, dances and a meal. Special clothes are worn.
Customs differ from one people to another: we learn them from elders and respect them.
lessons.model: An elder describes a traditional marriage in your culture: who speaks, what is offered, what is worn.
lessons.guided: Ask an elder about a marriage ceremony in your culture. Dramatise a short scene of the meeting of the two families.
lessons.exercise: What does a traditional marriage bring together?
lessons.remediation: Describe one element: the clothes or the gifts.
lessons.transfer: Tell your family what you learnt and ask about their own wedding.

practice.prompt: Which one is often part of a traditional marriage?
Draw the traditional dress worn at a marriage in your culture.
practice.answer: A drawing of a ceremonial dress.

practice.prompt: Act the meeting of two families with greetings in the family language.

lessons.title: Switching devices on and off correctly
lessons.objective: Demonstrate the process of powering on and off a computer, a tablet and a phone.
lessons.course:
To switch on a computer: check the cables, press the power button once, wait for the operating system to load. To switch off: save your work, close the programs, click Start then Shut down, wait until the screen is black, then switch off the socket if needed.
Never pull the plug while the computer is on: files can be lost or damaged. On a phone or tablet, hold the power button and choose “Power off”.
lessons.model: The adult shows the correct shutdown of a computer step by step.
lessons.guided: With an adult, switch on and shut down a computer or tablet correctly, saying each step aloud.
lessons.exercise: What must you do before shutting down?
lessons.remediation: Learn three steps: save, close, shut down.
lessons.transfer: Show a family member how to shut down a device correctly.
lessons.materials: A computer or tablet (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Put the shutdown steps in order.
Why must we not pull the plug while the computer is on?
choices: files can be lost or damaged
practice.answer: files can be lost or damaged

practice.prompt: How do we switch off a phone?
practice.answer: Hold the power button and choose Power off.
practice.explanation: Phones have a menu to power off.
